sweep_summary: Both title-hits are on target and were read in full. Bennett 2013 (Phonology 30: 355-398; CUP copy closed, author-hosted PDF open, saved) states the rule categorically ('Stress the ultima if heavy, otherwise the penult', p. 357) with lexical exceptions (25% of bisyllabic light-final nouns/adjectives oxytone, twelve antepenult nouns, no verbs; p. 358) but explicitly adopts Parker's description without critique. Parker 1998 (Glottolog 116705) is the UMass generals paper printed unrevised in GIALens 7(1) 2013; it was held by the project with a garbled text, which I decoded this search of works with stress in the title (font shift +1, U+F020 = space) so the passages are quotable: sec. 3.1 pp. 5-6 gives the same first-hand rule, quantifies the exceptions (56/225 = 24.9% of bisyllabic light-final nouns/adjectives), and pp. 22-23 add the twelve antepenult nouns and the three-syllable window. Also downloaded Bennett's 2013 handout (same facts) and re-read the catalog's Parker 1992 pp. 5-6 from the page scan, which confirm the catalog quote and correct three scanned misreads (tajpin, paloma, majshó; ríshquiti stressed on the antepenult). Not obtainable: Parker 1998b SIL WP 42 (not reachable by automated download; abstract says it is a duration study of coda [h], not stress placement; low priority) and Parker 1994 IJAL (paywalled DOI 10.1086/466224; medium priority, first-hand but redundant with 1998a for placement). new_statements.quote: To summarize our findings thus far, the basic pattern is that primary stress in Huariapano falls on the final syllable of the word if it is heavy (closed by a coda consonant), and otherwise on the penultimate. [...] Nevertheless, in spite of this basic, default pattern of penultimate stress in words whose final syllable is underlyingly open, there exist a number of exceptional forms which surface with primary stress on the final syllable, even though it is light. [...] within a list of 225 bisyllabic nouns and adjectives, 169 of them (75.1 percent) exhibit regular penultimate stress, whereas the remaining 56 words (24.9 percent) surface phonetically with stress on a light ultima [...] none of them are verbs.

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the fieldworker whose 1992 orthography note is the catalog's deciding source. weight-sensitive right-edge stress: closed final syllable takes stress ('always attracts the stress', p. 5); otherwise penult; word-final transitional [h]-type segments do not count as codas (fn. 5). Exceptions are lexical, not weight-driven: 24.9% of bisyllabic light-final nouns/adjectives are oxytone, twelve nouns are proparoxytone (pp. 22-23), no verb is exceptional, and primary stress always falls within the last three syllables. This turns the 1992 'normalmente.. normalmente' hedges into a categorical heavy-ultima rule plus a bounded, noun-only set of lexical exceptions; Bennett 2013 (pp. 357-358) restates the same facts as rule (5) 'Stress the ultima if heavy, otherwise the penult'. Consistent with the catalog's weight-sensitive coding; the 'hedged' element is best reclassified as lexical exceptions (roughly a quarter of light-final disyllabic nouns) rather than as uncertainty about the weight rule.

new_statements.quote: The fact that underlying coda consonants contribute a second mora to syllabic weight in Huariapano is easy to demonstrate. The assignment of primary stress is quantity-sensitive. In words which end with a light (open) syllable, stress defaults to the penultimate vowel in most cases. However, forms which end with a canonical coda consonant are regularly stressed on the ultima: (4) [examples glossed 'bow (weapon)', 'manioc', 'knees', 'opossum', 'bee'; IPA garbled in text layer] [...] In general this process [coda-[h] epenthesis in odd-numbered syllables] is totally oblivious to the presence, absence, or degree of stress in those syllables which receive a final [h].

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (Parker 1992: penult normally, ultima when the word ends in a consonant) and as the verified statement held by the project from Parker 2013 [1998] sec. 3.1: closed final syllable -> final stress 'regularly', open final -> penult 'in most cases'. Adds two compatible details: canonical codas are the three sibilants (final nasals often coalesce with the vowel), and instrumental evidence that stress does not lengthen vowels while epenthetic [h] behaves as a (somewhat short) moraic coda. Nothing here changes the weight-sensitive coding; the 'hedged' element again corresponds to lexical exceptions among light-final words.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is quantity-sensitive at the right edge: a word ending in a canonical coda consonant (the sibilants /s sh retroflex-sh/; syllable-final nasals often coalesce with the vowel and are set aside) is regularly stressed on the ultima; a word ending in a light (open) syllable takes penultimate stress 'in most cases' (i.e. lexical exceptions exist, not enumerated here; the author refers to Parker 1994 and Parker 1998 'Disjoint metrical tiers' for the full facts). Epenthetic coda [h] in odd-numbered syllables is independent of stress, and the instrumental result is that stress degree has no reliable effect on vowel duration while [h] adds roughly coda-like duration (analysed as a mora satisfying HEAVYFOOTHEAD in trochaic feet).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; chart (7) sorts vowels into three stress categories ('presence, absence, and/or degree of stress'; the category symbols are font-garbled in the text) and finds no durational difference among them. Feet are assumed trochaic (HEAVYFOOTHEAD) following Parker 1998a.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'in most cases' for penultimate stress in light-final words; no list of exceptional forms in this paper (they are treated in Parker 1998a / 2013 GIALens and Bennett 2013, already held by the project).
new_statements.identity_note: Huariapano = Panobo (ISO pno), extinct Panoan language of the lower Ucayali, Peru; data from the author's 1991 fieldwork with the last fluent speaker (two recorded oral texts), the same speaker/corpus behind Parker 1992, 1994 and 1998a.

sources.quote: In Huariapano, primary stress is quantity-sensitive and aligned to the right word edge, while secondary stresses are quantity-insensitive and show two patterns of directionality (discussed further below). The dominant primary stress pattern of Huariapano stresses the final syllable if heavy; otherwise, the primary stress surfaces on the penultimate syllable.

sources.quote: In Huariapano, main and secondary stress have opposite directionalities and quantity-sensitivity (Parker 1998). Main stress is assigned via a moraic trochee at the right edge of the word (88a, b). Default secondary stress is assigned via syllabic trochees starting from the left edge of the word (88c-e).

sources.quote: Huariapano, an extinct language of Peru, exhibits an unusual process of coda epenthesis by which the segment [h] is inserted in odd-numbered syllables of the prosodic word. [...] This article presents the results of an instrumental study which indicates that insofar as their relative duration is concerned, syllable-final [h]'s in Huariapano pattern as fully moraic coda consonants in keeping with the trochaic constraint HeavyFootHead.
sources.note: The only acoustic study of the language (rhyme/coda-[h] duration); bears on the moraic status of codas, i.e. the weight criterion behind the CVC-heavy coding; open on UND Scholarly Commons but an automated-access block blocks scripted download.
